entries.title: Trump’s Pick in Oklahoma Governor’s Race Wins His Primary
entries.summary: Former state Sen. Mike Mazzei beat Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond in a runoff, all but ensuring he’ll be the state’s next governor.
entries.content:
Former Oklahoma state Sen. Mike Mazzei is projected to win the Republican nomination for Oklahoma governor, giving President Donald Trump, who endorsed him, a win in one of his favorite states.

Mazzei defeated Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond, who has faced criticism from Trump and Gov. Kevin Stitt, in a primary runoff Tuesday runoff. He will face the Democratic nominee, Oklahoma state House Minority Leader Cyndi Munson, in November — but given the state’s red tilt, Mazzei is all but assured to win the governor’s mansion.

Mazzei entered the race in 2024 as an underdog compared to candidates such as Drummond, former state House Speaker Charles McCall and former Secretary of Public Safety Chip Keating. Compared to them, Mazzei had much less name recognition and a much smaller role in state politics.

However, after he spent millions of his own money and rose in the polls, he was endorsed by Trump just weeks before the initial June primary. This helped Mazzei advance to the runoff. That he’s won the nomination will give Trump a boost after a recent losing streak in gubernatorial primaries.

Stitt also chose to endorse Mazzei in the runoff. The governor’s relationship with Drummond grew toxic over their time in state politics.

Drummond and Stitt have publicly taken stabs at each other, including in court on tribal sovereignty and private charter schools receiving taxpayer funding.

This wasn’t always the case. At one point in their careers, the two had a good working relationship — both were wealthy men from the Tulsa area who ran in similar circles.

The relationship soured after Stitt picked John O’Connor over Drummond to fill what was left of former Attorney General Mike Hunter’s term after he resigned in 2021. O’Connor lost to Drummond two years later.

The animosity led to Stitt and much of his political team working to ensure Drummond didn’t become governor. While Stitt waited until the runoff lineup was set to endorse in the race, many of his staffers worked for other candidates in the primary.
entries.author: Reese Gorman

entries.title: Darline Graham Secures the Nomination for Senate Despite Late Campaign Gaffes
entries.summary: Graham’s win in South Carolina is a victory for President Donald Trump, who flew in to campaign for her and spent $800,000 on voter-outreach efforts.
entries.content:
Sen. Darline Graham defeated Rep. Ralph Norman for the Republican nomination for Senate in South Carolina, a victory that was also one for President Donald Trump, who pushed for her to stay on in the seat held recently by her late brother.

The Associated Press called the race at 9:02 p.m. Tuesday for Graham, whom Trump endorsed, campaigned for and backed with an $800,0000 last-minute effort from MAGA Inc. to turn out her voters.

“We got the vote out where we needed to,” senior Trump political adviser James Blair told NOTUS. “Great win for the President and for Darline.”

Norman had initially sought the South Carolina governorship and later bid for the open Senate seat, leaving South Carolina’s 5th Congressional District with an open race. The congressman is known for being adversarial at times to both House Republican leaders and Trump; Norman endorsing former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley in the 2024 presidential election and routinely criticizes his party’s agenda in Congress.

Graham’s win bolsters Trump’s influence ahead of the midterms, despite several candidates losing their primaries while carrying his endorsement.

Graham was appointed, at the president’s urging, to fill the remaining months of her brother Lindsey Graham’s term after his sudden death in July. Trump had touted her candidacy as a way to “honor the legacy of her beloved brother.”

Though there was little public polling ahead of the special election due to the tight timeline, a Trafalgar Group poll of the race released late Monday found the two candidates deadlocked at 48% each with a 2.9% margin of error. Some Republicans began to view a Graham victory as increasingly unlikely, NOTUS reported, after some campaign missteps.

In a televised debate on Aug. 18, Graham said she was “not that informed on national security” — a statement that stands in sharp contrast to her late brother’s deep investment and hawkish positions on foreign policy. The blunder was quickly picked up by Norman, who billed himself as an experienced “true conservative” while casting Graham as a candidate propped up by “left-wing Democrats.”

Trump traveled to South Carolina on Friday to stump for for Graham, urging voters to "pretend, please, that I'm on the ballot." When asked about her awkward answer in the debate, Trump told reporters, "All she was is being honest.”.

South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster appointed Graham to serve the remainder of her brother’s Senate term and officially endorsed her for the full term ahead of the runoff election.

Lindsey Graham’s passing left Republicans scrambling to find a replacement because the late, four-term senator had already won the primary for his seat in June. The Republican field quickly expanded to 10 candidates — including Graham, Norman, Rep. Russell Fry, businessman Mark Lynch and Mark Sanford, the former congressman and governor.

The most prominent candidates knocked out in the primary split their endorsements, with Fry backing Graham and Sanford and Lynch throwing their support behind Norman.

Graham will face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews in November in the general election for the Senate seat, which is rated “Solid R” by the Cook Political Report.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: Hasan Piker Roils Michigan Senate Race
entries.summary: Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed has tried to distance himself from the left-wing streamer’s recent comments about Jewish Americans, but some lawmakers say it’s not enough.
entries.content:
Streamer Hasan Piker’s comments about Jewish Americans’ support for Israel are still haunting Abdul El-Sayed’s Senate campaign, as the Michigan Democrat tries to distance himself from the growing backlash within his own party.

Piker’s broadcasts, which frequently include criticism of the Israeli government, have become a trip wire for moderates eager to denounce him before conservative opponents can tie his commentary to their own campaigns. Democrats’ quick condemnation this week shows how toxic associating with Piker has grown on the Hill — a risk for swing-state candidates like El-Sayed, who has campaigned with the streamer before.

“Hasan Piker is an antisemite,” Rep. Josh Gottheimer (D-New Jersey) said on Fox News on Tuesday. “Nobody should be anywhere near this guy. Nobody should campaign with him or repost him. Frankly, anyone who is quiet right now is complicit.”

A new wave of Piker criticism began when an audio clip resurfaced last week, appearing to feature Michigan state Sen. Jeremy Moss saying his campaign’s main objective is ensuring the U.S. continues its support for Israel. While Moss says the audio used is fake, Piker spoke about the video during a Monday stream — arguing that Jewish Americans’ continued support for Israel promotes the idea that the community is “monolithic,” thus opening them up to violence.

“If Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone’s going to come around and take action — not against the state of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews,” Piker said.

Moss initially said he was not going to endorse El-Sayed unless the Senate candidate increased outreach to his district’s Jewish community. The state senator backed out of doing so following Piker’s stream, Semafor reported.

El-Sayed’s connection to Piker, with whom he campaigned ahead of the August primary, has followed the Senate candidate’s race throughout the summer — even as the Democratic nominee tries to separate himself from the streamer’s comments.

“I want to be crystal clear, nobody speaks for this campaign besides me and my campaign spokespeople,” El-Sayed wrote in a statement.

But a slate of Jewish Democrats said Tuesday that they think El-Sayed needs to take a stronger stance against Piker and further disavow the streamer’s rhetoric before it tanks the Senate candidate’s campaign altogether.

Rep. Brad Schneider (D-Illinois), who chairs the New Democrat Coalition, criticized El-Sayed for what he sees as refusing “to condemn the words of Hasan Piker, his friend and frequent campaign surrogate.”

“It is disingenuous for El-Sayed to try to distance himself from Piker without specifically condemning, refuting, or even just rejecting Piker’s hateful rhetoric,” Schneider wrote in a press release Tuesday. “Claiming that no one speaks for him except himself and his team is not enough.”

Gottheimer on Tuesday reiterated his call to pass his resolution denouncing antisemitic rhetoric from online personalities like Piker and Candace Owens, a measure he introduced in April with Rep. Mike Lawler (R-New York).

El-Sayed’s potential Senate colleagues also weighed in: Sen. Jacky Rosen (D-Nevada) said that while Piker has been “trafficking in antisemitic tropes for a while,” his recent statement “is a new low.”

“In a time where political violence and anti-semitism has been spiking — and where just 6 months ago Michigan had a nearly deadly event of anti-semitic mass violence at Temple Israel — no one should causally be suggesting that anyone, Jews or otherwise, are to blame for being targeted,” Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Michigan) wrote on X.

During a Tuesday news conference meant to address a rise in Islamophobic rhetoric, El-Sayed took a moment to denounce antisemitism and uplift Judaism, which he called “a beautiful faith that rhymes with so much of my own.”

“Insofar as there are disagreements about foreign policy, my hope is that folks understand where those disagreements align and also understand that that does not come at the cost of Jewish safety,” the Democrat said, referencing earlier conversations with Moss.

El-Sayed’s news conference came after Jake Lang, a self-described anti-Islamic activist and Jan. 6 riot participant, held protests this month in Dearborn, home to the highest proportion of Muslims in the country. The Senate candidate has faced Islamophobic rhetoric leading up to the general campaign, and spoke on Tuesday alongside other statewide candidates and religious leaders.

Republican opponent Mike Rogers has tried to court Jewish voters who may be hesitant to back El-Sayed over his criticism of Israel, but those efforts have so far seen limited success.

Meanwhile, a number of other congressional Democrats have pushed to disavow Piker’s language as the party grapples with growing divisions among voters on sending military aid to Israel.

“There is a bright line between vigorous debate and rhetoric that stokes hatred toward our neighbors. Mr. Piker has crossed that line, repeatedly and unmistakably,” Sen. Cory Booker (D-New Jersey) said in a statement.

Rep. Hillary Scholten (D-Michigan) was one of the first Democrats to speak out against Piker and defend Moss. She told reporters on Tuesday that El-Sayed — whom she has not endorsed — had “not reached out to me yet. If he would, I would have some questions,” referencing the candidate’s “past associations” with Piker.

Scholten and Piker exchanged heated messages Monday on X after the congresswoman called his comments “unacceptable.”

Piker hit back on X, calling Scholten “an israel 1st congresswoman” who was “vying for the spotlight.”

“There’s only one of us hurting the chances of a Democratic majority in November…and it ain’t me!” Scholten replied.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: Trump Wants Unity in Georgia. The Blood May Be Too Bad.
entries.summary: Discussions over the lieutenant governor’s endorsement, which included an offered ambassadorship, appear stalled by a spate of unresolved legal squabbles.
entries.content:
Germany was on Burt Jones’ mind.

President Donald Trump had offered to make the Georgia lieutenant governor the ambassador to one of Europe’s largest countries — an extravagant, if common, consolation for a Republican rebounding from a primary loss. But Trump wanted something in exchange for the new gig: for Jones to endorse Rick Jackson, the Republican nominee for governor, people familiar with the conversations told NOTUS.

Because Jones has been unwilling to acquiesce, the appointment is in doubt, those sources said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to detail private deliberations.

In recent weeks, Trump has sought a détente between Jones, an ardent ally who received the president’s endorsement for governor in December, and Jackson, the political upstart, to unify the party behind Jackson. Jackson is now in a close contest against former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms to succeed Gov. Brian Kemp, a Republican who is term-limited.

Jackson and Jones met a few weeks ago at Trump’s urging, according to a person familiar with the dynamics, with the president hoping they could overcome Jones’ anger to resolve their differences. The person added that the meeting was cold and unproductive. A spokesperson for Jackson’s campaign confirmed the meeting took place and said Jackson would welcome Jones’ support in the election.

Jones’ camp, the people familiar said, has their own demand for any potential endorsement of Jackson: a lawsuit settlement valued around $25 million. The pair traded lawsuits during the primary. Jones’ family’s gas company sued Jackson for defamation in June. The suit accused Jackson of using the company’s branding to make false claims about Jones. It sought $100 million in damages.

Jackson has sued Jones twice. The first was a federal lawsuit to restrict spending from Jones’ leadership committee. The second was a defamation lawsuit after Jones’ campaign accused Jackson’s business of working with Planned Parenthood.

Jones loaned his campaign $25 million.

“The president did ask Lt. Governor Jones and Rick Jackson to meet, but nothing was offered in exchange,” a spokesperson for Jones said in a statement to NOTUS. The spokesperson did not respond to a follow-up question clarifying whether Trump offered Jones the ambassadorship.

The White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Trump endorsed Jackson after he won the runoff and praised him at an event in Georgia last month. Georgia Attorney General Chris Carr, who also ran for governor, endorsed Jackson before the runoff. But Jones has refused to endorse until his legal disputes with Jackson are resolved.

Also in the meeting with Jones and Jackson was Jones’ father, Bill Jones. A successful Georgia businessman, the elder Jones financially backed his son’s campaign. At least part of the endorsement resistance comes from him, according to the people familiar, who described a dynamic in which Jones’ father holds significant sway.

Trump has appointed multiple failed Republican candidates to positions within his administration during his second term, with an emphasis on ambassador roles. Two were candidates in Georgia: David Perdue, the ambassador to China, and Herschel Walker, ambassador to the Bahamas.

Georgia has consistently caused headaches for Trump. In 2018, Democrats flipped a Republican congressional seat outside of Atlanta and almost won the governor’s mansion. During the 2020 cycle, Republicans lost both Senate seats, and Joe Biden defeated Trump by the slimmest of margins to turn the state blue for the first time since Bill Clinton in 1992.

Although it returned to red in 2024, some Georgia Republicans are concerned that affordability issues, the Iran war and Trump’s broader unpopularity could allow Democrats to gain ground this year. Republican Rep. Mike Collins’ campaign for Senate has struggled to gain traction against Sen. Jon Ossoff, Democratic candidates are campaigning heavily in deep-red areas and multiple polls have found Bottoms running just ahead of Jackson.

Two of the people familiar said Jackson needs Jones’ endorsement if he wants to beat Bottoms.

“I don’t believe he can win without Jones’ endorsement,” said one of the people. “I don’t know if he can win with it, to be honest. But he definitely can’t win without it.”

Jackson’s spokesperson said that the Republican Party is “rallying around Rick Jackson to support him in our upcoming election against Keisha Lance Bottoms.”

Some are more bullish on Jackson’s chances and downplayed the significance of getting Jones’ public support. Eamon Keegan, a Republican pollster in Georgia, said that it wasn’t uncommon for Democratic candidates in the state to have an edge in summer polling, only to underperform in November.

“People have moved on from the primary runoff now,” Keegan told NOTUS, though he added that it wouldn’t hurt for Jones to endorse Jackson. Keegan said he expects “any Burt Jones supporter will be on Team Jackson on or before November 3rd.”
entries.author: Ben T.N. Mause

entries.title: Political Operatives Warn Campaigns: Don't Trust Prediction Markets
entries.summary: Prediction market companies are trying to get their foot in the door as traditional polling falters.
entries.content:
The slow decline of traditional polling has left politicos, who are always desperate for numbers, in a lurch.

Two venture-backed prediction market companies are offering nothing short of magic to meet those needs: real-time odds on who will win elections, and even projections of how much they will win by. As these companies lean into aggressively gamifying — or rather, gamblifying — U.S. politics, political operatives are warning campaigns not to take them seriously.

“The thing we have to remember is they're not in any way representative of the voters that decide elections,” said Steve Schale, a Democratic strategist. “It is sort of like degenerate gambling for political hacks.”

Schale likened polls to “heroin” for people in politics. Prediction market projections offer more numbers for that demographic to obsess over, but that doesn’t make them helpful to campaigns, he argued.

Elections are big business for prediction markets. South Carolina’s Senate Republican primary runoff between Sen. Darline Graham and Rep. Ralph Norman saw more than $25.7 million in trading activity on Kalshi. The platform projected Graham’s odds at around 56% when polls closed, and she won.

Prediction markets, which claim to reflect the “wisdom of the crowd,” have missed the mark several times this primary season though: Last Tuesday, Kalshi’s market completely floundered in Florida’s Senate Democratic primary — it projected that insurgent democratic socialist state Rep. Angie Nixon had single-digit chances of winning. She won by a lot: The Associated Press called the race right as polls closed in the state.

In Wisconsin’s Democratic gubernatorial primary on Aug. 11, David Crowley pulled off an upset, even though Kalshi projected for weeks a single-digit chance of him winning.

The day before Abdul El-Sayed so narrowly clinched his victory in the Senate Democratic primary in Michigan, Polymarket projected his chances of winning at more than 98% — and the market on his victory margins predicted it would be a blowout, with him winning by at least 15%. That mirrored polls ahead of the election, which showed El-Sayed with a double-digit lead over his opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens. He won by less than 1 percentage point.

“It seems to me now that they're much more reaction markets than prediction markets,” said Eddie Vale, a Democratic political consultant who works with Crowley’s campaign. “The theory was, if people had to put money or skin in the game, sort of the collective wisdom and knowledge was going to help predict things, but it's pretty clear that people are just betting in reaction to seeing the news, seeing a new poll.”

“Anybody that has experience on campaigns knows that they're useless,” Vale said of prediction market odds.

Prediction market platforms are forcing their way onto social media feeds through partnerships, including with newsrooms like CNN and Fox, and political influencers like Gunther Eagleman, a conservative poster with 1.7 million followers. Kalshi and Polymarket, the two biggest prediction platforms where people can trade event contracts, futures and derivatives on real-world events, are leaning into the political realm — both even have dedicated midterms betting hubs.

But the people who actually work around campaigns and politics have balked at some of the marketing.

Adam Carlson, a progressive pollster and prolific political poster, said he’s been approached with offers for paid partnerships with prediction markets. He said that while he personally finds prediction market odds “interesting,” he never checks on any candidate’s odds of his “own free will.”

“Polling can exist without prediction markets. Prediction markets cannot exist without polling,” Carlson said. “There is some value to them directionally, but there are some very clear weaknesses … It's just more like a conversation starter if you're not involved in the campaign. Or, it's a discourse generator.”

One conservative strategist, Liz Mair, told NOTUS that she does see prediction markets changing politics because more people are being exposed to them — which can change how operatives think about running campaigns.

“The main change I'm seeing is that a lot of people who should know better are treating the odds offered by prediction markets as a substitute for polling. That's a huge mistake,” Mair said in an email to NOTUS. “While there's a lot wrong with polling … there's zero reason why the opinions of a bunch of randos that skew prediction markets should be treated as remotely indicative of outcomes.”

Sure, polling has its issues, as both pollsters and political operatives conceded in interviews for this story. But they still generally have transparent methodologies, and strive for representative samplings that provide campaign operatives with nuanced, actionable data about where they’re falling short.

Only 14% of Americans report placing bets on prediction markets “sometimes” or “frequently,” according to a Navigator Research survey conducted in April. And those who do tend to be young men.

Prediction markets and polls also measure different things: Polls often ask people who they’d vote for, whereas markets ask who people think will win. For people running campaigns, the markets are more of a vibe check than a prognosis.

“A real poll is digging deep into their opinion on certain issues. That's what drives things: ‘How do you feel about the economy? How do you feel about the price of gas? Should we be at war in Iran?’ Yada, yada, yada — a good pollster can read through all those and pull a result out. Well, none of that is in Kalshi,” Jacob Perry, a Democratic strategist, said.

Elisabeth Diana, Kalshi’s head of communications, said the platform is “more, actually, accurate than polling,” and pointed NOTUS to a Washington Post analysis of 2,000 primary election markets that found that despite several high-profile misses, markets were generally accurate, meaning candidates given a 75% chance of winning won around 75% of the time. The company has also done its own research to argue that its markets are accurate.

“We see prediction market forecasts as an effective complement to polling — it's an additional data point that surfaces wisdom-of-the-crowd data, and it's historically very well-calibrated,” Diana said in a statement.

The company has paid people to post about the betting platform on X, marketing it as something that could replace polls entirely, in an apparent effort to capitalize on people’s frustrations with traditional polling.

“Kalshi just released its new Midterms Hub, and it may be the final nail in the coffin for traditional polling,” Overton News, a news aggregator and Kalshi partner, posted on X. “The same pollsters who were embarrassingly WRONG about the 2024 election.”

While operatives and strategists warn against making campaign decisions based on the platforms’ projections, some said it can be used to fundraise, since it can make donors feel better about a candidate’s viability. The Democratic Senate candidate in Alaska, Mary Peltola, used her Kalshi odds to argue that her campaign has “a 57% chance to beat the DC establishment and take back Alaska” in a post on X earlier this month. The Senate Majority PAC, a super PAC aligned with Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, boasted in an email fundraising bid last month about Kalshi’s projections showing that Democrats have a chance of taking back the Senate.

“Because they update hourly, well, literally, minute by minute, they're a very attractive, shiny object to rely on. But we don't have decades of experience with how accurate they are, in the same way that we have many decades of experience with polling, both for good and bad," said Charles Franklin, the director of Marquette Law School Poll. “It's a wildly unrepresentative sample of the public.”

Given that prediction market bettors are largely on the younger side, could operatives’ dismissal of their worth speak to a generational gap? Mandy Zhang, a Gen Z Democratic digital strategist, said that while her friends use prediction markets for fun, nobody treats them like they’re prophetic.

“Digital teams do pay attention to where their candidates are sitting on these platforms, mostly as a quick pulse check or another data point. But I don’t think anyone I’ve worked with treats them as the ‘holy grail’ of political forecasting. They’re something people look at and talk about, but not something campaigns are necessarily building their strategy around,” Zhang said in a message to NOTUS. “Working across different campaigns this year, I’ve seen firsthand that they can be pretty wrong.”

Matthew Bartlett, a Republican strategist, said that if he were advising a campaign this year, he would tell them: “My short advice? Stay away.”

“You have so many people, just like sports betting is almost as big as sports, the betting markets are almost as big as politics themselves, and when you're talking about real, human events such as sports or elections, they're prone to disruption,” he said. “Win by the polls, die by the prediction markets.”
entries.author: Emily Kennard

entries.title: Democrats Embrace 'Redboxing' Loophole in Hot Congressional Races
entries.summary: Candidates can’t legally coordinate with outside groups. But they can publish messaging wish lists that deep-pocketed super PACs act on.
entries.content:
In Texas’ toss-up U.S. Senate race, Democrat James Talarico routinely trashes “billionaire mega-donors” and big-money politics.

But buried inside Talarico’s campaign website is a messaging wish list for super PACs inclined to produce and run ads supporting his campaign against Republican Ken Paxton. Among Talarico’s asks: Tell Texas voters he supports capping insulin costs and “affordable prescription drugs from Canada” and opposes “puppet politicians.”

Lone Star Rising PAC, a super PAC primarily funded by billionaire LinkedIn founder Reid Hoffman, responded to the Talarico campaign’s bat signal. It spent hundreds of thousands of dollars this year across major Texas media markets on an ad praising Talarico’s advocacy for “cap[ping] the cost of insulin at $25” and “affordable prescription drugs from Canada” while fighting against “puppet politicians.”  

More than a dozen Democratic candidates in the nation’s hottest congressional races have embraced “redboxing,” a controversial election-season technique that provides super PACs and other moneyed outside groups with campaign materials without, technically, violating federal laws against coordination.

Five of these candidates removed “redboxing” content after inquiries from NOTUS.

Such materials, which are sometimes surrounded by a red box on the campaign website, include messaging priorities and specific instructions for where and how to spend on advertising, according to a NOTUS analysis of campaign websites for candidates in the closest House and Senate races as rated by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report.

At least one Republican candidate also features a “redboxing” memo, as do Democratic and Republican party committees, which are barred from directly coordinating messaging with super PACs.

Critics have characterized “redboxing” as an effort to circumvent anti-coordination laws, which were put in place to insulate campaigns from potential political influence from donors or groups. The practice is either patently “illegal” or, at least, violates the “spirit of campaign-finance regulation,” argue some supporters of stricter campaign finance rules.

But the Federal Election Commission, the government agency that interprets and enforces federal campaign finance laws, has previously determined that “redbox” requests posted publicly, such as on a website, and available to a general audience do not count as illegal coordination.

Democratic and Republican political operatives alike acknowledge that in practice, the average voter is not in a position to act on “redboxing” requests, nor are they the intended target. Super PACs and other outside groups, in contrast, may have hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars in reserve to help get their preferred candidate elected — and they’re on the lookout for campaigns’ wink-wink, nod-nod guidance.

The FEC has been effectively sidelined from making any new rulings this election cycle because it doesn’t have enough commissioners to cast binding votes.

In the nation’s closest congressional races, significantly more Democrats than Republicans use “redboxing” messages on their websites this year, NOTUS’ review indicates.

Democratic campaign websites with specific messaging and distribution requests include Jamie Ager in North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District, Christina Bohannan in Iowa’s 1st Congressional District, Rep. Kathy Castor in Florida’s 14th Congressional District, Pia Dandiya in Florida’s 22nd Congressional District, Christina Hines in Michigan’s 10th Congressional District, Bobby Pulido in Texas’s 15th Congressional District and Tom Suozzi in New York’s 3rd Congressional District. None of the campaigns responded to requests for comment.

Castor campaign website (2082x1376, AR: 1.51) Pia Dandiya campaign website (1756x580, AR: 3.03)In New Hampshire, three candidates vying for the Democratic nomination in the state’s 1st Congressional District are using “redboxing” ahead of their Sept. 8 primary: Stefany Shaheen, Carleigh Beriont and Maura Sullivan.

Sullivan’s media page says her “name should come up within the first five seconds of any ad.”

A recent video ad from super PAC Vote Vets waits a little longer — 11 seconds — before mentioning Sullivan by name. But the ad incorporates several specific themes and details from Sullivan’s “redboxing” page, including that she waited tables in college, served in Iraq and would fight corruption. Both the “redbox page” and Vote Vets ad use the phrase “new generation of leadership.”

Sullivan spokesperson Emmett Avery declined to comment. Representatives for Shaheen and Beriont did not respond to repeated messages.

Five Democratic candidates pulled down their redbox-style media pages after NOTUS reached out for comment: Reps. Vicente Gonzalez of Texas, Adam Gray of California and Gabe Vasquez of New Mexico; Randy Villegas in California’s 22nd Congressional District; and William Lawrence in Michigan’s 7th Congressional District.
Vicente Gonzalez campaign website archive (1532x1230, AR: 1.25)“We have no comment at this time,” Lawrence spokesperson Mya Legel said in an email to NOTUS. The Gray, Gonzalez, Vasquez and Villegas campaigns did not respond to several requests for comment, including on their decisions to take down the redbox-style pages.

The “Media” tab on Villegas’ campaign website now redirects to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee’s “redboxing” page for the race, which includes specific talking points and a list of ZIP codes to target for digital advertising.

Party committees are also legally prohibited from coordinating with outside groups. The DCCC has “redboxing” pages for more than a dozen other competitive races, including “toss-up” races in Arizona’s 6th Congressional District, New Jersey’s 7th Congressional District, Texas’ 34th Congressional District and Washington’s 3rd Congressional District.

“The messages we post on these pages are intended for the general public and are fully consistent with the law and FEC guidance,” DCCC Communications Director Courtney Rice said in an emailed statement to NOTUS.

Talarico’s “redbox” page, which his campaign updated and slimmed down in mid-August, previously stated it was “most important” to reach voters in the San Antonio, Austin and Harlingen-McAllen media markets.

The Lone Star Rising PAC aired its ads in each of these markets and several more, including Dallas-Fort Worth and Houston. Collectively, prospective voters have seen the ad nearly 1.9 million times, according to political ad tracking firm AdImpact.

The Talarico campaign did not respond to several requests for comment. Lone Star Rising PAC also did not respond to requests for comment.

A few Republicans in key contests have also used “redboxing.”

The National Republican Congressional Committee, the party committee supporting House Republicans, has its own “redboxing” page with specific instructions and requests for spending in competitive races.

The NRCC page for the “toss-up” race in Ohio’s 9th Congressional District reads: “It’s imperative that voters are educated on Toledo broadcast, streaming and in their mailboxes districtwide, particularly in Henry, Putnam, and Paulding Counties (which are in the newly drawn OH-09), that [Rep. Marcy] Kaptur has voted for far-left policies that are out of [sic] out-of-touch and make our communities less safe.”

The NRCC did not respond to requests for comment from NOTUS.

And in Florida’s 25th Congressional District race, Republican candidate Scott Singer’s campaign website published a memo last month with information on “How Voters Need to Receive Positive Information on Singer.” The Singer campaign does not link to the memo through a “Media Kit” or other vague label, as others do, but within the image of a thin line at the bottom of the campaign website — an unusual placement that a general audience would be less likely to notice.

Saurav Ghosh, director of federal campaign finance reform at Campaign Legal Center and a former enforcement attorney at the FEC, is one of the leading critics of “redboxing.” There is no exception explicitly written into the law for coordination via public platforms, Ghosh argues, and the practice undermines anti-coordination law that’s intended to ensure independence.

But “when big money is directly underwriting campaigns,” Ghosh told NOTUS, “you end up with Congress, White House, an elected government that is directly indebted to big money interests, and nothing could be more corrosive to everyday Americans having a voice and being actually represented in their government.”

Sean Cooksey, a former Republican FEC commissioner, dismissed Campaign Legal Center’s stance as “pearl-clutching.”

“Redboxing is not illegal,” and is “not a threat to democracy,” Cooksey told NOTUS via email. “I believe free speech is fundamental to democratic government and individual liberty.”

As recently as 2022, Cooksey and his former colleagues at the FEC, including Trump-ousted Democratic commissioner Ellen Weintraub, dismissed a complaint brought by Campaign Legal Center alleging coordination between a campaign and super PAC through social media.

When asked about candidates such as Talarico who campaign on getting big money out of politics but have these redboxing pages, Ghosh said it’s “a messaging point that maybe the candidates genuinely believe.”

“But for purposes of their own campaign and how they’re conducting their efforts to get elected, it's clear that if they’re redboxing, they are asking super PACs to support them,” Ghosh said.
entries.author: Taylor Giorno, Dave Levinthal

entries.title: Dolly’s D.C. Legacy
entries.content:
Good morning. This is the NOTUS Metro newsletter for Aug. 26, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

If you raised a child in D.C. over the past decade, you may have a closer connection to Dolly Parton than you think.

The beloved country music star, who died Tuesday, was the driving force behind D.C.’s Books from Birth program, which sends free books to District kids every month through their fifth birthday. The program is part of Parton’s Imagination Library, which she created in 1995 to spur interest in reading and has mailed out more than 300 million books.

More than 4 million books have been sent to almost 100,000 kids in D.C. over the past decade. Roughly 77% of kids under the age of 5 in D.C. have enrolled in the city’s program — among the highest rates of all the areas that Imagination Library serves.

“We are profoundly indebted to her,” Richard Reyes-Gavilan, the executive director of the D.C. Public Library, said in a statement posted to social media, “not only for her timeless music and cultural influence, but for her unwavering belief that every child deserves access to books and the opportunities they create. … We will always love Dolly Parton.”

Parton’s Imagination Library is also available in Montgomery County and Prince George’s County, and there are efforts to bring it to Northern Virginia.





FROM THE DISTRICT

Kennedy Center demolition? The conflict between preservationists and the Trump administration over the fate of the iconic performing arts center is heating up, with administration lawyers telling a federal judge that the venue may have to be demolished if President Donald Trump’s renovation plans — and the proposed two-year closure to complete them — are blocked, NOTUS’ Jenna Monnin reports. Were that to happen, the attorneys added, the Kennedy Center could be replaced by an outdoor amphitheater.

D.C.’s housing market could use a little fuel, but maybe not this literally. The Washington Business Journal reports that a former Sunoco gas station at 15th and U streets Northwest is likely to become just another gas station, after plans to convert the site to housing fell through. A developer worried that they couldn’t make the economics work, a stark indicator of the headwinds the city’s housing market is facing due to a slowing economy and complaints about local regulations and bureaucracy.  

The long-awaited, $92 million 11th Street Bridge Park project may soon accept contractor bids, City Cast D.C. reports. The park’s director expects to break ground by the end of the year.





FROM VIRGINIA

Loudoun County Board of Supervisors member Juli Briskman told WTOP that she’s running for chair next year with a focus on “stopping data centers.”

Amtrak will have a nine-day service outage in October affecting routes south of D.C.’s Union Station, NBC4 reports. A key rail part that helps trains switch tracks needs to be replaced. During the disruption, buses will help commuters get to or from places like Alexandria, Richmond and Roanoke.





PLAN YOUR WEEKEND

Peirce Mill Square Dance (2304x1536, AR: 1.50)
For cat lovers: CatVideoFest 2026 at AFI Silver, Thursday.

For folksy folks: Summer Square Dance at Peirce Mill, Saturday.

For old friends: “Merrily We Roll Along” at Signature Theatre, ongoing.

For more info on this weekend’s events, read our weekly culture calendar here.





SPORTS

Is this training camp or Training Day? NOTUS’ Martenzie Johnson reports that new Commanders defensive coordinator Daronte Jones has turned to a unique source of inspiration this summer: Oscar-winning actor Denzel Washington. Jones, a big Denzel fan, often tells his defensive players to put their “Denzel Washington caps on,” meaning they need to disguise their intentions before a play.

“We want to make every [coverage] look the same,” Jones said. “That requires putting on our best acting hat.”

The Big Ten will pass a rule prohibiting its members from using the much-discussed eligibility loopholes that have allowed some football players to move from the professional game back down to college, according to ESPN. Sorry, Terps — no boomerang additions for you.

What to Watch Today

MLB: Nationals vs. Rockies, 6:45 p.m. (MLB.TV)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@notus.com.

The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson. Photo courtesy of Bill Mills. One last thing: that $1.5 million house we showed you yesterday is located in Virginia.

entries.title: Win for Graham, and Trump Too
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Graham and Trump claim victory. Kalshi had it right, this time. A new term for you: redboxing. And: A Georgia grudge may be holding up an ambassadorship.





THE LATEST

Donald Trump orchestrated Darline Graham’s appointment to her temporary seat, dropped into Myrtle Beach to stump for her and shoved a rare $800,000 in campaign cash to get out the vote — so they could both revel in victory last night as she claimed the Republican nod seeking a full, six-year Senate term. Trumpworld was quick to claim credit.

“We got the vote out where we needed to,” senior Trump political adviser James Blair told NOTUS’ Kadia Goba. “Great win for the President and for Darline.”

The president really wanted this win after story after story about his endorsement lacking firepower. Graham, who paid tribute to her late brother Lindsey after the race was called, gave the president his due: “South Carolina is truly Trump country.”

Voters made clear Graham was their thing — Rep. Ralph Norman even lost in parts of his own congressional district. His concession speech was one for the history books.

"I hate it for the state,” Norman said, noting that while he’d accept the outcome, he didn’t understand why the president got involved in the race. “I really hate it for the state. I don’t hate it for me. I don’t hate it for the family — we’re going to be fine. But we did this for service, and I hate it for the state.”

Trump also notched another victory last night with his primary pick in the Oklahoma governor’s race where former state Sen. Mike Mazzei earned the Republican nomination.

Score one for the prediction markets, too. Kalshi saw more than $25.7 million in trading around the South Carolina runoff, with Graham’s odds at around 56% when polls closed. NOTUS’ Emily Kennard dives into how prediction markets are playing a major role in the political sphere this cycle, even if most politicos aren’t yet sold on the new tool. As one strategist quipped to her, the online sites are “like degenerate gambling for political hacks.”

Open tabs: Trump’s Trade War Gives Republicans Another Midterm Headache (NOTUS); Trump Plans to Buy Midterm Ads About His Own Record (Atlantic); Pennsylvania reports first 2 measles deaths in the US this year, both people unvaccinated (AP); Ex-School Board Chair Wins Race to Fill David Scott’s House Seat in Georgia (NYT); FEMA crew broke law by skipping homes with Trump signs, watchdog says (WaPo)





From the campaign trail


Wish-list Wednesday: Democrats have made a point of calling out big-money politics this cycle. But buried on many of their campaign websites, NOTUS’ Taylor Giorno and Dave Levinthal report, are wishlists that many have been using to skirt federal laws against coordination with megadonors. The so-called “redbox” sends a not-so-subtle message: In case you have the money to spend, here’s where and how we’d suggest doing so.

Democratic and Republican political operatives agreed that the redboxing requests are a wink-wink, nod-nod at those super PACs and outside groups that have the big cash to spend.

And on the cash note, NOTUS’ Avani Kalra reports that while dozens of Democratic candidates have pledged to reject donations from corporate political action committees, in reality, a simple workaround is enabling the flow of money from business interests to the campaign accounts of those very same candidates.

By accepting contributions from Democratic leadership PACs, the candidates who have called for getting money out of politics have been able to benefit from that corporate cash. Some money-in-politics experts say there isn’t the same level of influence between candidate and corporate cash as there is with money from leadership PACs. One operative told Avani that while the corporate cash and leadership PAC money is different, they are two tiers to the same flow of cash.

From the White House


When Trump offered to make Burt Jones the U.S. ambassador to Germany, the president asked for one thing in return: for Jones, who had lost to Rick Jackson in the Republican primary for Georgia governor, to endorse his former rival.

NOTUS’ Ben T.N. Mause reports that Jones has been unwilling to make that deal, putting his nomination in doubt. Sources familiar told Ben that Jones’ team had its own demands in return for an endorsement, including a $25 million settlement over lawsuits the two filed against each other in the primary. The blood, it seems, may just be too bad.





ON NOTUS PODCAST

From your favorite podcast app: Our reporters spent time on the campaign trail with House Speaker Mike Johnson as he works to keep his majority and his leadership post. Reporters Oriana González, Reese Gorman and Kadia Goba shared their reporting on how each party is making its pitch.





NOTUS PERSPECTIVES

The better things look for Democrats in 2026, writes Matt K. Lewis, the worse they could be in 2028.





NOTUS METRO

Sign up for our local newsletter, written by Martin Austermuhle and Zara Norman.

Local news: What to Do in the D.C. Area This Weekend, by Rebecca Ritzel

Sports desk: How Denzel Washington Is Helping the Commanders Build Their Defense, by Martenzie Johnson





NEW ON NOTUS

A federal immigration agent who is at the center of an interstate clash after he shot a Venezuelan man earlier this year has discussed plans to relocate to a Mexican beach town with his extramarital girlfriend, NOTUS’ Jose Pagliery reports.

Minnesota attorneys, who are seeking to extradite ICE agent Christian Castro to face charges in the state, raised the discussions to a federal judge in court records. Gov. Greg Abbott has declined to allow the agent’s transfer from Texas.

More: Trump Asks the Supreme Court to Back Asylum Ban at U.S.-Mexico Border, by Jackie Llanos

Hasan Piker Roils Michigan Senate Race, by Jenna Monnin





NOT US

  • Top Commanders Told Hegseth Not to Cut Civilian Protection Program, Poll Showed. He Did It Anyway. By Megan Rose and Hannah Allam for ProPublica
  • The County Prosecutors Who Became ICE Informants, by Aura Bogado for Wired
  • Many N.F.L. Players Get Brain Disease. Why Hasn’t OSHA Intervened? By John Branch for The New York Times

entries.title: How Denzel Washington Is Helping the Commanders Build Their Defense
entries.summary: New defensive coordinator Daronte Jones wants to disguise coverages. That requires a bit of acting.
entries.content:
It appeared Lions quarterback Joshua Dobbs had a quick and easy throw to make.

In the first quarter of Saturday’s preseason game against the Commanders, Dobbs looked across the line before the snap and saw seven defenders itching to blitz him, three defensive backs in man-to-man coverage, and a single safety sitting 20 yards back. The math would tell him that getting the ball out fast could lead to a big-yardage play.

But when the center snapped Dobbs the ball, only four of the would-be blitzers rushed. The other three joined defensive back Antonio Hamilton Sr. in zone coverage about 10 yards away, with the remaining three defenders another 10 yards behind them in a deeper zone.

So Dobbs had to improvise. He ran to the right, planted his feet and threw across his body toward the middle of the field, right into the hands of Washington safety Quan Martin.

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

That’s the beauty of defensive coordinator Daronte Jones’ scheme: You may think the Commanders are doing one thing, but they’re actually doing something else completely.

And who is to credit for that exceptional pre-snap acting job against Detroit? Denzel Washington.

The Academy Award-winning actor, famously known for playing Coach Herman Boone in the 2000 movie “Remember the Titans,” has no actual connection to the Commanders. He’s never given the team a pep talk or appeared at Northwest Stadium.

But Jones often invokes Washington when teaching his players the importance of disguise. He wants his players to become Hollywood actors, showing one thing (say, all-out blitz), but then switching to something completely different (seven dropping back into coverage) after the snap. Jones constantly tells players to “put your Denzel Washington caps on.”

“I think he's one of the best actors to ever do it,” Jones said. “And so that was just referencing how we have to sell our disguises, make every look, look the same. That requires putting on our best acting hat.”

Against Detroit, the defense often acted as if they were in a Cover 1 scheme, which meant man coverage for the cornerbacks and one safety providing help over the top. This approach normally makes a defense more susceptible to a long pass. But they were actually in Cover 3, which uses zones rather than man to prevent chunk yardage plays.

Daronte Jones AP - 26042035958002 (8066x5378, AR: 1.50)
There are all kinds of ways to disguise a defense. A cornerback can disguise zone coverage by lining up right on the receiver before backing off at the snap. A safety can rotate from being 20 yards off the ball to playing more like a linebacker. Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores, whom Jones worked under from 2023 to 2025, had 322-pound defensive tackle Domonique Orange drop back into coverage last week against the Ravens. It’s all about causing chaos for the opponent.

Disguising coverage isn’t a new phenomenon. But with modern offenses using more shifts, motions and run-pass options to confuse the defenses, disguises can provide a counterpunch that stalls the offense, even just for half a second.

“A lot of the quarterbacks in the league can read coverages,” defensive back Car’lin Vigers said. “But disguising it, making them second guess something, checking into something that they shouldn't have checked into, it gives us the advantage.”

Not every play is as heavily disguised as the Dobbs interception: Amik Robertson’s strip sack of Dobbs on the second play of Saturday’s game was clearly a cornerback blitz. But for a defense that ranked near the bottom of the league in nearly every category, the returns through two preseason games are promising. The unit has allowed 109.5 passing yards per game, had five sacks and forced five turnovers. Last season, the defense caused just 10 turnovers, second worst in the NFL.

“It shows your high level of IQ,” cornerback Mike Sainristil said of the defense’s ability to confuse the offense. “The more we’re able to do that as a defense, the more plays we’ll get.”

But the “Denzel Washington caps” do more than just expose offenses — they also expose the age gaps within the team.

Jones, 47, was introduced to Washington after his grandfather had him watch 1984’s “A Soldier’s Story.” Jones is also a fan of 1989’s “Glory.” Millennials on the team skew more toward Washington’s early 2000s output like “Remember the Titans” (2000) and “Training Day” (2001). And the younger Gen Zers are most familiar with the “Equalizer” trilogy (2014 to 2023) and “Fences” (2016).

“Denzel got a whole lot of movies, and it's crazy I'm on the spot and just can't even think of them,” the 26-year-old Vigers said when asked about his favorite Washington flick.

Jones wouldn’t be shocked by that admission.

“Most of them are probably so young they don't even know who Denzel is,” he said with a tone of defeat.

entries.title: How Corporate PAC Money Gets to Democrats Who Swore It Off
entries.summary: In swing-district contests around the country, candidates who took pledges not to take corporate PAC money are still benefiting from it.
entries.content:
Democratic candidates' call to get money out of politics is a central theme in the 2026 midterms, with dozens of Democratic incumbents and candidates pledging to reject donations from corporate political action committees.

But there’s a workaround that is enabling the flow of money from business interests into the campaign accounts of many Democrats who otherwise reject cash from corporate PACs.

Candidates, particularly those in the most competitive races, are relying on contributions from Democratic leadership PACs — groups formed by federal lawmakers to boost their party’s congressional candidates. And many of those leadership PACs receive significant donations from corporate PACs.

Daniel Lobo-Lewis, a co-founder of the Political Integrity Project, which grades candidates based on their financial transparency and anti-corruption commitments, told NOTUS the practice is “an issue.”

“No American voter, if you ask them, ‘Do you want corporations to be able to give money, have more power?’ will say yes,” Lobo-Lewis said. “That extends to leadership PACs in the same way” as corporate PACs.

Political entities established by House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, House Democratic Whip Katherine Clark and House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar are among the committees that have donated to “no corporate PAC money” candidates while receiving donations from corporations such as banking giant Barclays, pharmacy chain CVS and insurance company UnitedHealthcare this year. Jeffries, Clark and Aguilar did not respond to requests for comment from NOTUS.

One Democratic political operative who has worked on campaigns that chose to reject corporate PAC money, and who requested anonymity to discuss the decision-making process, said it’s actually relatively easy for Democratic challengers to reject corporate money.

“Very few corporate PACs are going to want to give money to a Democrat running either against a Republican [incumbent] or in an open seat to begin with, so not taking corporate PAC money should be an easy choice for Democratic challengers in any cycle,” the operative told NOTUS.

It’s harder to forgo leadership PAC contributions, the operative said, which can help candidates build support within the Democratic caucus and get to know their potential future colleagues.

Cait Conley, who is challenging Republican Rep. Mike Lawler in a New York district the Cook Political Report has deemed a “toss-up,” is one of the candidates who pledged not to accept corporate PAC money.

But nearly half of the contributions that Conley received from federal PACs came from committees that took corporate PAC money. Conley received $5,000 from the Jobs, Education and Families First PAC (JEFF PAC), which is tied to Jeffries, and another $5,000 from the New Democrat Coalition Action Fund, for example.

Both of those committees took contributions from corporations, including from defense companies such as Honeywell International and Lockheed Martin. Conley, who spent 16 years as an active-duty Army officer and later worked for the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, has made national security a major part of her campaign messaging.

Conley’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment from NOTUS.

Rebecca Bennett, who is challenging Rep. Tom Kean Jr. (R-New Jersey) in another “toss-up” district, has also vowed not to accept corporate donations.

Federal filings show Bennett nonetheless took $5,000 from JEFF PAC and another $1,000 from BEEPAC, along with other leadership PAC donations. Connecticut Rep. Jim Himes, the top Democrat on the Intelligence Committee, created BEEPAC and has accepted contributions from those defense companies and others such as RTX Corporation.

Bennett has similarly spotlighted her experience as a Navy veteran and has pledged to help improve the Defense Department’s technology development to ensure service members “have the equipment and capabilities they need” if she is elected to Congress.

Bennett’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment from NOTUS.

https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/EEKWw/1/
Conley and Bennett are not alone. Other swing district candidates in similar situations include Paige Cognetti and Bob Brooks in Pennsylvania and Randy Villegas in California.

Michael Beckel, a money-in-politics expert at nonprofit Issue One, told NOTUS that there’s a big difference between taking corporate and leadership PAC money, since companies don’t have the same access to and influence over lawmakers when money goes through a leadership PAC instead of directly to a candidate.

“Forgoing corporate PAC money is breaking a point of connection between a company seeking friends and allies in Washington,” Beckel said. “If that money is flowing through a leadership PAC to benefit them, the original corporate donor isn’t getting any of the benefits of directly donating.”

And End Citizens United, the group that initiated these pledges in 2018, also insisted that taking money contributed by leadership PACs does “not, in any way, equate to accepting corporate PAC money.”

“As the organization that established the no corporate PAC pledge, we can unequivocally confirm that Democratic candidates are abiding by their commitment to reject corporate PAC money,” spokesperson Bawadden Sayed said.

Republicans still outpace Democrats when it comes to donations from corporate PACs, though the gap is narrowing. In 2024, the top 20 business and corporate PACs gave about 55% to Republicans and about 45% to Democrats, an analysis by public affairs firm Quorum found.


https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/YVReo/1/
According to data from OpenSecrets, the nonpartisan watchdog group, contributions by Democratic leadership PACs to candidates are on the rise.. The committees gave $24 million to candidates before June 30 –– up from nearly $21 million by that time in 2024 and nearly $19 million in 2022.

Republican candidates receive more leadership PAC donations than Democrats, as well. As of June 30, Republican candidates had received $34 million in contributions from those groups, as opposed to Democrats’ $24 million.

https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/BHGdr/1/
Lobo-Lewis, whose group sponsors its own “anti-corruption” pledge for lawmakers and candidates, maintained that Democratic candidates should eventually go further when it comes to rejecting money from any business interests aiming to influence policy in Washington.

“That pool of money is definitely dirtied by the corporate money,” Lobo-Lewis said. “The first step in this anti-corruption fight is getting rid of direct corporate donations, and then going after the leadership PACs, joint fundraising committees and eventually the super PACs as well.”

An increasing number of Democratic incumbents in safer blue seats are also benefiting from leadership PAC donations as they avoid directly taking corporate money.

Some Democratic lawmakers who have taken the pledge say it can be “demoralizing” to run a campaign without corporate money ahead of what is expected to be the most expensive midterm in election history.

Rep. Josh Riley of New York, whose race the Cook Political Report has deemed “likely D,” has taken money from groups such as Blue Momentum PAC, associated with California Rep. Ted Lieu, and the Serve America PAC, affiliated with Massachusetts Rep. Seth Moulton. Those entities received contributions from companies including BlackRock, General Electric and Google.

“Josh Riley has never accepted a dime of corporate PAC money, and he never will,” senior campaign advisor Mauranda Evans told NOTUS in a statement. “His vote is not for sale."

The Democratic operative who requested anonymity to talk about making these decisions said he thinks taking corporate money is completely different from taking leadership PAC money, but he expects the issue will continue to be a point of disagreement among Democrats.

“This gets to the root of a major problem in American politics, and that is the influence of corporate and dark money that we have,” the operative said. “Until we pass something at a federal level to get corporate money out, to get dark money out, that tension is still going to exist in one way or another.”

entries.title: What to Do in the D.C. Area This Weekend (Aug. 28)
entries.summary: It’s the closing weekend for The Playground and CatVideoFest, and opening weekend for “Merrily We Roll Along.”
entries.content:
Thursday 


Taffety Punk’s “Freddie: A Girl” at Capitol Hill Arts Workshop

545 7th Street SE, 8 p.m., $20

A small but mighty local theater company begins performances of a new play based on Freddie and Truus Oversteegen, teen sisters who join the Dutch resistance and become spies, saboteurs and assassins who shoot Nazis from their bicycles. Lise Bruneau, a local theatermaker with Broadway credits, directs. Thursday and Friday’s performances are discounted previews. “Freddie: A Girl” opens Saturday and runs through Sept. 19 at the intimate black-box space on Capitol Hill.

CatVideoFest 2026 at AFI Silver

8633 Colesville Road, Silver Spring, 11:30 a.m., $8-10

Every office has that coworker who’s always ready with a cute animal video (or GIF). This film screening is for them, and other cat lovers. Each year, Oscilloscope Laboratories collects the most fantastic feline clips on the internet and rolls them into one long, adorable package. Cinemas then partner with local rescues to host screenings. Thursday is your last chance to support City Dogs and City Kitties by catching CatVideoFest at AFI.

More to explore: Bluegrass trio Chatham County Line at Jammin’ Java.

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Friday 


Chamber Music With the Kennedy Center Opera House Orchestra 

The Justice Forum at The Reach, 2700 F Street NW, 6 p.m., free

Closed or not, the Kennedy Center is contractually obligated to continue paying members of its Opera House Orchestra, who normally perform with touring ballet companies, musicals and other special events (in addition to their gigs with the Washington National Opera). So why not let them play for the public? Friday the musicians offer an hour of music by Dvořák at The Reach. The repertoire includes his inspired-by-Iowa “American” String Quartet No. 12 in F Major and his lively Bagatelles, Op. 47.

Maraca Bruja at National Geographic Museum of Exploration 

1600 M Street NW, 6 p.m., $20

When the National Geographic Museum of Exploration opened in June, the DMV didn’t just gain a museum, it gained a world-music concert series. The Friday night Concerts in the Courtyard continue this week with Maraca Bruja. The New York-based collective focuses on music of Colombia’s Caribbean coastline. Members play a variety of instruments, including the gaita, an indigenous flute made from hollowed-out cactus stems.

More to explore: Sango and New Impressionz Band at La Cosecha in Union Market

Saturday 


Summer Square Dance at Peirce Mill

2401 Tilden Street NW, 7 p.m., free

Do-si-do with or without a partner at the annual Square Dance sponsored by Friends of Peirce Mill and held on the grounds of D.C.’s only functioning gristmill. First-timers and fans of contra dancing (plus all related folk dance forms) will all swing round and round beneath strings of lights in Rock Creek Park.

Culture Quest Kids Fest at Deanwood Recreation Center

1350 49th Street NE, 3 p.m., free

A trio of D.C. government organizations with very long names — the Mayor’s Office on African American Affairs, the D.C. Department of Parks and Recreation and the D.C. Commission on the Arts and Humanities — team up to sponsor a daylong community festival for families.

More to explore: “Klex,” six 10-minute plays inspired by one work of art, at The Stacks.

Sunday 


The Playground closes at the National Building Museum

401 F Street NW, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. $16 to $19

The Building Museum’s annual summer installation gives families a chance to keep kids clean and active while escaping the heat. This year, the museum commissioned an imaginative play space from the New York firm Snarkitecture. Sunday marks the final day of the installation. Small adventurers can navigate a 100-foot obstacle course, climb a 15-foot wall, chill in rope hammocks, shoot hoops, wander through a maze and tunnel through a “dig pit” full of cork pieces, all in one air-conditioned place.

“Merrily We Roll Along” at Signature Theatre

4200 Campbell Avenue, Arlington, 2 p.m. and 7:30 p.m., $47 to $97

“Merrily We Roll Along” traces the lives of a trio of friends in reverse, and rather famously flopped on Broadway when it opened in 1981. But “Merrily” gained pop-culture momentum after it was featured in the film “Lady Bird” and was revived on Broadway in 2023, in a production that starred Jonathan Groff, Lindsay Mendez and Daniel Radcliffe. Shirlington’s Signature Theatre, which specializes in Sondheim musicals, began previews for “Merrily” on Tuesday and the show runs through Nov. 1.

More to explore: James Taylor opens a three-night stand at Wolf Trap. Sunday is sold out, but tickets remain for Tuesday and Wednesday.
